title: The Lewis & Clark Expedition
summary: Put the Corps of Discovery's 1804–1806 journey in order, name the people who made it possible, and ask what it meant for the Native nations along the way.
challenge: In 1804, President Jefferson sent a team called the Corps of Discovery to explore the huge new land west of the Mississippi River, all the way to the Pacific Ocean. What did they do first, next, and last — and who helped them along the way? Follow the trail and put the journey in order.

event.title: Lewis & Clark Expedition
event.place: St. Louis to the Pacific Ocean

moments: 1804 (May 14) — The Corps sets off up the Missouri River near St. Louis.
1804–1805 (winter) — The Corps builds Fort Mandan; Sacagawea joins the group.
1805 (summer) — The Corps crosses the Rocky Mountains with Shoshone and Nez Perce help.
1805 (November) — The Corps reaches the Pacific Ocean and builds Fort Clatsop.
1806 (Sept 23) — The Corps returns safely to St. Louis.
people: Sacagawea (Lemhi Shoshone) — interpreter who helped guide and trade
York — Clark's enslaved man, a full working member of the Corps
Corps of Discovery — about 45 soldiers and explorers
Mandan, Hidatsa, Shoshone & Nez Perce nations — hosts who gave food, directions, and horses
mapData.why: The journey mapped a huge new part of the country, recorded hundreds of plants, animals, and Native nations, and opened the West to more American travel and settlement.
mapData.question: How did the Native nations along the trail feel about the strangers crossing their homelands — and what happened to those nations afterward?

teacherText.keyideas: The expedition (1804–1806) mapped about 8,000 miles round trip, recorded plants, animals, and Native nations, and strengthened U.S. claims to the West. Sacagawea (Lemhi Shoshone) and York (an enslaved man) were vital members. The Corps could not have succeeded without food, directions, and horses from Native nations.
teacherText.misconceptions:
• Lewis and Clark did not 'discover' empty land — Native nations had lived there for thousands of years.
• Sacagawea did not single-handedly guide the whole trip; she interpreted and helped at key moments.
• The expedition did not find an all-water route to the Pacific — no Northwest Passage existed.
teacherText.vocabulary: Corps of Discovery, Louisiana Purchase, expedition, interpreter, Northwest Passage, Fort Mandan, Fort Clatsop.
teacherText.context: Departed near St. Louis May 14, 1804; wintered 1804–05 at Fort Mandan (met Sacagawea); crossed the Rockies in summer 1805 with Shoshone and Nez Perce help; reached the Pacific in Nov. 1805 (Fort Clatsop); returned to St. Louis Sept. 23, 1806.
